total-fertility-rate-s1.title: Total fertility rate in two countries

table.caption: Births per 1,000 women per year in each 5-year age group, Country C, 2020 (invented data for practice)
Average years of schooling for women, infant mortality and total fertility rate in five countries (invented data for practice)

items.q: In about which year did Country B’s total fertility rate first fall below replacement level?
options: Between 1980 and 1990
Between 1960 and 1970
Between 2000 and 2010
It stays above replacement through 2020

why.correct: Find where the line crosses the dashed replacement level.
options: Right: it was 2.2 in 1980, just above 2.1, and 1.9 in 1990, below it.
In 1970 Country B’s TFR was 2.9, still above 2.1.
By 2000 it was already 1.7, below replacement.
From 1990 on, it is below the 2.1 line.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in Country A’s total fertility rate from 1960 to 2020, then give the answer, rounded to one decimal place.

mistakes.why: That is the change in children per woman. Divide by 6.8 and multiply by 100.
That divides by 2.8. Divide by the starting value, 6.8.
Divide by the starting value, 6.8, not 2.8.

items.q: Country A’s TFR in 2020 is 2.8. What does this predict for its population, if nothing else changes?
options: It will shrink, because the TFR has been falling
It keeps growing: 2.8 is above 2.1
It holds steady, since 2.8 is close to 2
It will double each year from now on

why.correct: Compare TFR with about 2.1 to predict long-run growth or decline.
options: A falling TFR still above 2.1 means slower growth, not decline.
Right: each generation more than replaces itself.
Replacement is about 2.1; 2.8 is well above it.
A TFR of 2.8 means growth, but nowhere near doubling each year.

items.q: Country B has been below replacement since about 1990. Which long-run problem is it most likely to face?
options: Too few schools for a growing number of children
Rapid population growth that outruns its food
Fewer workers and a larger share of older people
A sharp rise in infant mortality

why.correct: Low fertility over decades shrinks young cohorts and ages the population.
options: Below-replacement fertility means fewer children, not more.
A TFR of 1.5 means the population will tend to shrink.
Right: fewer births mean smaller young cohorts, so in time fewer workers support more retirees.
A low TFR does not cause infant mortality to rise.

items.q: Each age group in the table covers 5 years. Calculate Country C’s total fertility rate: add the rates, multiply by 5, and divide by 1,000.

mistakes.why: You forgot the × 5. Each rate is per year, and each age group lasts 5 years.
You did not divide by 1,000. The rates are per 1,000 women.

items.q: Country C’s total fertility rate is 2.16. How does it compare with replacement level?
options: Well below it, so the population will shrink fast
Far above it, so the population will grow fast
Exactly 2, so the population will hold steady
Slightly above, so slow growth
2.16 is not below 2.1.
2.16 is only a little above 2.1.
The TFR is 2.16, and replacement is about 2.1, not 2.
Right: 2.16 is just above about 2.1.

items.q: In which age group do women in Country C have the most births per 1,000?

why.correct: Read the largest value in the column: 130, ages 25 to 29.
options: Right: 130 births per 1,000 women per year, the highest in the table.
20-24 has 120, just below the 25-29 group.

items.q: What relationship does the table show between women’s years of schooling and total fertility rate?
options: As schooling increases, TFR increases
As schooling increases, TFR decreases
There is no relationship between them
TFR is highest where schooling is highest

why.correct: Describe the direction of the relationship, with the end values.
options: TFR falls as schooling rises.
Right: from 2 years and 6.1 children down to 13 years and 1.6.
TFR falls steadily across the five countries.
Country T, with the most schooling, has the lowest TFR.

items.q: Which explanation best links infant mortality to the total fertility rates in the table?
options: Low infant mortality makes families want more children
Infant mortality and TFR are unrelated
Where many babies die, families have more births
High TFR causes infant mortality to fall

why.correct: When fewer children die, parents need fewer births to raise the family size they want.
options: The table shows lower infant mortality with lower TFR.
They fall together across the five countries.
Right: Country P has 85 infant deaths per 1,000 and a TFR of 6.1; Country T has 4 and 1.6.
The pattern runs the other way: high TFR goes with high infant mortality.

items.q: By how much is Country P’s total fertility rate above replacement level, taken as 2.1?

why.correct: Subtract replacement level: $6.1 - 2.1 = 4.0$ children per woman above replacement.

mistakes.why: That uses 2 as replacement level. Replacement level is about 2.1.
That adds 2.1. To find how far above, subtract: 6.1 - 2.1.

items.q: What is replacement-level fertility in a country where few children die young?
options: Exactly 2.0 children per woman
About 3.5 children per woman
About 1.0 child per woman
About 2.1 children per woman

why.correct: About 2.1 where child deaths are low; higher where they are high.
options: Two would replace two parents only if every child survived to adulthood.
That is well above replacement; the population would grow.
One child per woman halves each generation.
Right: just over 2, to make up for children who die young and the slight excess of boys at birth.

items.q: Which changes usually lower a country’s total fertility rate? Select all that apply.
options: More girls finish secondary school
The legal age of marriage is lowered
More families depend on children to work on farms
Infant mortality rises sharply

why.correct: Education, family planning and lower infant mortality lower TFR; earlier marriage, child labor on farms and high infant mortality raise it.
options: Right: schooling delays marriage and widens choices.
Earlier marriage adds years of child-bearing, which raises TFR.
Children as farm labor raise the value of large families, raising TFR.
High infant mortality tends to raise TFR.

items.q: Explain how more years of schooling for women tend to lower the total fertility rate.

why.correct: Schooling, later marriage and work, fewer children, lower TFR.

cause.label: Change
options: stay in school longer
marry younger
work on family farms

why.1: Younger marriage tends to raise fertility.
why.2: Children working on farms makes large families more useful, raising fertility.

effect.label: Effect
options: tend to marry later and take paid jobs
tend to marry earlier
stop using family planning

why.1: Schooling delays marriage; it does not hasten it.
why.2: Schooling makes family planning more likely, not less.

mechanism.label: Result
options: they have fewer children over their lifetimes, lowering the TFR
they have more children, raising the TFR
the TFR stays the same

why.1: Later marriage and paid work lower the number of children.
why.2: Later marriage shortens the years of having children, which lowers TFR.

specific.model: When women stay in school longer, they tend to marry later and take paid jobs, so they have fewer children over their lifetimes, lowering the TFR.

items.q: A country wants to lower its high total fertility rate without forcing anyone. Which policy is most likely to work, based on this topic?
options: Free schooling for girls, and clinics
Paying families a bonus for each new child
Lowering the legal age of marriage
Closing clinics that care for infants

why.correct: Expanding education and choice lowers fertility without force.
options: Right: both lower TFR by expanding choice, and both have worked in many countries.
Payments per child tend to raise fertility.
Earlier marriage tends to raise fertility.
Higher infant mortality tends to raise TFR, and it harms children.

items.q: A country’s total fertility rate falls from 2.4 to 2.0 over ten years, but its population is still growing. Which explanation is best?
options: A TFR of 2.0 means fast growth
Large young cohorts now have children
The TFR was measured wrongly
Fewer babies are born each year than before

why.correct: TFR describes family size; momentum describes the number of parents.
options: A TFR of 2.0 is below replacement; growth here comes from momentum.
Right: population momentum keeps growth going after TFR falls below replacement.
There is no need to assume an error; momentum explains it.
Fewer births would slow growth; the explanation is the size of the parent cohorts.

items.q: In Country S, the TFR is 2.0 and infant mortality is 8 per 1,000. If its TFR stays at 2.0 for many decades, with no people moving in or out, what will most likely happen to its population?
options: It will grow rapidly over the long run
It stays the same size for good
It slowly declines in the long run
It will double in size about each 35 years

why.correct: Below about 2.1 means, in the long run and without migration, a shrinking population.
options: A TFR below replacement does not produce rapid growth.
Just below replacement means a slow decline in the long run.
Right: 2.0 is just below replacement, so each generation is slightly smaller.
That would need a growth rate of about 2% a year.
